Power BIGroup project of five

Survey About KIU Students

Business question
How do KIU students perform, live and spend? Five research questions: GPA by gender, faculty and course; lifestyle (housing, work, stress management); scholarships and expenses; sleep and its link to GPA; GPA by faculty and academic year.
Data
A student survey with 343 respondents: 216 Management, 108 Computer Science and 19 Mathematics students.
What the dashboard shows
A decomposition tree for exploring GPA by faculty, course and gender. Pie, donut and stacked charts for lifestyle. Combined column and line charts for tuition and scholarships. A key influencers visual and an average GPA gauge (2.95 on a 1.2 to 4.0 scale), with slicers for faculty and course.
Findings
86% of respondents live on campus. Friends are the most common way to handle stress (20.4%), followed by music (14.4%). Average sleep is similar across faculties, at about 6.3 to 6.6 hours.

PythonEnd-to-end analysis

What drives life expectancy across income groups?

Business question
How do wealth, health spending, education spending and infant mortality relate to life expectancy in countries at different income levels?
Data and cleaning
Five World Bank indicators for 21 countries in four income groups, 2000 to 2020 (441 country-years). Education spending was missing in 32% of rows, so I filled gaps by interpolation within each country, capped outliers with the IQR rule and ran a data quality report before and after.
Analysis
New features: log GDP, a Health Burden Index and Human Capital Investment. Nine charts, then three models predicting life expectancy and a K-Means clustering of countries.
Findings
Infant mortality has the strongest link to life expectancy (correlation -0.94), ahead of GDP per capita (0.77), health spending (0.60) and education spending (0.20). Random Forest predicted best (R² 0.98), ahead of Linear Regression (0.93) and Decision Tree (0.93). Low-income countries gained the most, rising from about 56 to about 67 years between 2000 and 2019, which narrowed the gap with high-income countries.
Limits and next steps
Infant mortality is itself a health outcome and carries about 90% of the Decision Tree's feature importance, so the model scores partly reflect that. Next I would split the data by country before cleaning and test other cluster counts.

TableauGroup project

Formula 1: growth, dominance and reliability

Business questions
How has Formula 1 grown over time? Which drivers and constructors are the most successful? How does reliability (DNFs) differ by constructor and country? Does grid position influence the result? Which constructors are expected to perform best in the future?
Data and calculations
The Formula 1 World Championship dataset (races, results, drivers, constructors, circuits), 1,125 races and 802 drivers. Results were classified as finished or did not finish, then used to calculate DNF rate per constructor and average DNFs per race by country, with fixed LOD expressions. Country names were standardised and missing positions filled.
Findings
Races per season rose from about 7 in 1950 to about 24, while the number of drivers per season fell from over 100 in the 1950s to about 20 to 25 today. Hamilton and Schumacher lead in career wins, and Ferrari, McLaren and Mercedes lead among constructors. Starting closer to the front goes with better finishing positions. The forecast shows McLaren growing but Ferrari leading in later years.

R ShinyGroup assignment of five students

Health Investment & Outcomes dashboard

Business question
Does spending more on health lead to better outcomes? Six research questions, one chart each, across 11 countries including Georgia, 2002 to 2022.
Data and build
Indicators pulled live from the World Bank API in R, cleaned and merged by country and year, with health spending adjusted to constant 2015 USD. The app has a year-range slider, a country selector and a top-N control.
My part
I wrote most of the code, including the World Bank data pulling and the infant mortality analysis (research question 4, with its chart and written analysis). Teammates built the other research questions and charts, and their names are credited in the code.
Findings
Infant mortality fell in every country. Georgia improved fastest, from about 25 to about 8 deaths per 1,000 between 2002 and 2022, overtaking Brazil and Mexico, which ended near 13. Developed countries started and stayed low. Across all countries, health spending per capita and life expectancy have a correlation of 0.58, and life expectancy is clearly higher in developed countries (median 81 years against roughly 73 in developing ones).
